originalGroup.material:
The painting I nearly hid

At our school art sale, I displayed three finished paintings and left a fourth under the table. It showed a harbour at dawn, but the boats were only pencil ____1____. I had never added their colours.

A visitor noticed its corner. Before she could pull it out, I said, "That one isn't ____2____."

"May I look anyway?"

I showed it to her, explaining where I had stopped. She studied it more ____3____ than she had studied the finished pictures. I expected a list of faults.

Instead, she asked why I had chosen that view. I described sitting beside my grandfather, peacefully watching the sky brighten while the boats remained dark. As I spoke, I remembered the ____4____ that had made me start painting.

The visitor said the pencil lines helped her imagine how the picture had ____5____. Her son was learning to draw and often believed that a good painting appeared perfectly at the first attempt. She wanted him to see a stage ____6____ the beginning and the finished work.

I offered to add the colours before she collected it. She ____7____, taking a moment before answering. "Only if you want to. Please don't finish it just to make it look more expensive."

We agreed on a small price and wrote a note clearly identifying it as a work in ____8____. I did not want anybody to mistake it for something I had completed.

After she left, I took a photograph for my records. The empty space no longer looked simply like ____9____. It showed a choice I had not yet made.

I still finish most of my paintings. But I have stopped ____10____ every incomplete page as though it proves I cannot draw. Some are useful studies; others need another attempt. What matters is being ____11____ about their stage and purpose.

The sale did not turn unfinished work into an excuse to avoid ____12____. It helped me see that learning has visible ____13____. A visitor had asked a better question than "Is it finished?" She had asked how it ____14____. That conversation gave me the courage to put a sketchbook on the table at the next sale, with its working pages ____15____.

Two kinds of directions

Grandpa asked me to help him use the new ticket machine at the station. He usually bought tickets from a person, but wanted to ____1____ the machine himself.

I explained the screens ____2____, pointing at one button after another. He asked me to ____3____ the first step. I sighed and reached forward to do it for him.

"I'm trying to learn," he said.

His quiet words stopped me. I had mistaken being fast for being helpful. Grandpa looked ____4____ because I had given several instructions before he could try the first one.

I stepped back and ____5____ him one action. Then I waited while he tried it ____6____. When he selected the wrong screen, we returned to the start. I explained more ____7____ instead of taking over.

After one more ____8____, he bought the correct ticket. The machine was not suddenly ____9____, but he now knew where to begin. He kept the ticket and suggested a short walk before the train arrived.

Outside, I could not find the path to the old bridge. Grandpa ____10____ it clearly, pointing to a narrow lane beside a café. He had walked there long before the station entrance moved.

I was ____11____ by how easily our roles had changed. At the machine, I had knowledge he needed. Outside, his experience guided me. Neither kind made the other person's ____12____ unimportant.

On the bridge, I thanked him for reminding me to show ____13____ when helping. He smiled. "Then explain the machine again on the way back," he said. "Just a little more ____14____."

We laughed. Next time he would try without me beside him. That afternoon, however, we had found our way ____15____, each giving the other enough time to understand.
